questiontext.text:
Which sentence best summarises the direct proof above, including why it proves the proposition for every real number \(x\)?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A direct proof starts from what is known and reaches the conclusion by steps that are valid for every value of the variable. Here the known facts are the rules for multiplying out brackets, which hold for all real numbers, so the conclusion holds for all real numbers. That is the second sentence.

  • Substituting \(x = 1\) shows only that the two sides are equal when \(x = 1\). No single value, or finite list of values, covers every real number.

  • Starting from the statement to be proved and simplifying it is circular: it assumes what was to be shown. Simplifying a false statement can also lead to something true: from \(1 = -1\), squaring gives \(1 = 1\).

  • A graph shows only what you can see, to the accuracy of the drawing, and different curves can look the same. The algebraic proof works exactly, for every value of \(x\).

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the direct proof of x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) by multiplying out the brackets (pp. 5-6) in Section 2 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Yes. The argument never uses a particular value of \(x\), and every rule it uses is true for all real numbers, so it proves the proposition for every \(x\).
